Then He said, Most High: ﴿and the moon has split﴾, meaning "and the moon has already split." It was also said: ﴿and the moon has split﴾ means the matter became clear and manifest, and the Arabs use the moon as a metaphor for what is clear. A poet said:

Stand up, sons of my mother, and rest your riding beasts,
for I am inclined to a tribe other than you.
The needs have been fulfilled while the night is moonlit,
and the saddles and riding beasts have been tightened for the journey.

It was also said: the splitting of the moon is the splitting of darkness from it by its rising within it, just as dawn is called "falq" (daybreak) because darkness splits away from it. Its emergence is sometimes expressed by "splitting," as al-Nabighah said:

When they turned their backs with a clamour among them,
a caller called us at the splitting of dawn.

I say: It has been established by the transmission of trustworthy individual narrators that the moon split in Makkah, and this is the apparent meaning of the revelation. It does not follow that people must be equal in witnessing it, because it was a nocturnal sign, and it occurred at the request of the Prophet (ﷺ) to Allah, Most High, at the time of the challenge. It is narrated that Hamzah ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, when he embraced Islam out of anger at Abu Jahl's insulting of the Messenger (ﷺ), asked to be shown a sign by which his certainty in his faith would increase. It has already been mentioned in the Sahih that the people of Makkah were the ones who asked and demanded to be shown a sign, so he showed them the splitting of the moon into two halves, as in the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud and others. It is narrated from Hudhayfah that he gave a sermon in al-Mada'in and then said: "Indeed the Hour has drawn near, and the moon has split in the time of your Prophet (ﷺ)." It has also been said that it is by inversion of order, its meaning being "the moon split and the Hour drew near," as Ibn Kaysan said. It has already been mentioned from al-Farra' that when two verbs are close in meaning, you may place one before the other, at His saying: ﴿Then he drew near and descended﴾ [[See p. 89 of this part.]].

His saying, Most High: ﴿And if they see a sign, they turn away﴾. This indicates that they saw the splitting of the moon. Ibn 'Abbas said: The polytheists gathered before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "If you are truthful, split the moon for us into two parts, half over Abu Qubays and half over Qu'aiqi'an." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to them: "If I do it, will you believe?" They said: "Yes." It was the night of Badr. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked his Lord to give him what they had said, and the moon split into two parts, while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called out to the polytheists: "O so-and-so, O so-and-so, bear witness!" They asked them, and they said: "We have seen the moon split." Then this was revealed: ﴿The Hour has drawn near, and the moon has split. And if they see a sign, they turn away﴾, meaning: if they see a sign indicating the truthfulness of Muhammad (ﷺ), they turn away from faith. ﴿And say, "Continuous magic"﴾, meaning passing away, from their saying: "The thing passed and continued" when it went away. Abu al-'Aliyah and al-Dahhak said: firm, strong, intense, and it is from "mirrah," which means strength. As Laqit said:

until its twisted strength became firm upon a rope,
resolute in its determination, neither weak nor feeble.

Al-Akhfash said: it is derived from "imrar al-habl," which means the intensity of twisting a rope. It was also said: its meaning is "bitter," from "marārah" (bitterness). One says: amarra al-shay' (the thing became bitter), and likewise marra al-shay' (with fatha) became bitter, so it is murr; and others caused it to be bitter (amarrahu and marrahu). Al-Rabi' said: continuous, effective. Yamani said: passing. Abu 'Ubaydah said: false. It was also said: lasting. A poet (the verse is by Imru' al-Qays, whose first hemistich is: "Verily the world is nights and days") said:

and nothing upright remains lasting,

meaning, does not last. It was also said: some of it resembles other parts, meaning the actions of Muhammad have continued in this manner, so he brings nothing that has a true reality; rather, all of it is imagination. It was also said: its meaning is that it has passed from the earth to the sky.

﴿And they denied﴾ our Prophet ﴿and followed their desires﴾, meaning their misguidance and their choices.

﴿And every matter is settled﴾, meaning it settles with every doer for what he did: the good settles with its people in Paradise, and the evil settles with its people in Hellfire. Shaybah read "mustaqarr" with a fatha on the qaf, meaning every thing has a time in which it occurs without advance or delay. It is narrated from Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' "wa kullu amrin mustaqarrin" with kasra on the qaf and the ra', making it an adjective of "amr," and "kull" in this case may be nominative as a subject with an omitted predicate, as if he said: "And every matter is settled in the Mother of the Book, existing." It may also be nominative by conjunction with "the Hour," the meaning being: "The Hour has drawn near and every matter is settled," that is, the settling of affairs on the Day of Resurrection has drawn near. Whoever reads it nominative makes it the predicate of "kull."

﴿And there has certainly come to them of the news﴾, meaning from some of the news. He, glorified be He, mentioned of it what He knew they needed, and in which there is healing for them. There were matters beyond this, but He related to us what He knew we need, and remained silent about the rest. This is His saying: ﴿And there has certainly come to them of the news﴾, meaning there came to these disbelievers some of the news of the earlier nations ﴿that which contains a deterrent﴾, meaning what would restrain them from disbelief had they accepted it. Its original form is "muztajar," then the taʼ was changed to dal, because ta' is a voiceless letter and zay is a voiced letter, so the ta' was replaced by a dal which agrees with it in articulation point and agrees with the zay in voicing. "Muzdajar" is from "zajr," which means restraint; one says: zajarahu and izdajarahu, so he was restrained and refrained (infazara and izdajara), and I restrained him so he was restrained (zajartuhu fa-infazara), meaning I held him back so he held back, as the poet said:

So he became one whose pursuit of the courtesans
was restrained from his desire by restraint.

It was also read as "muzzajar," by changing the ta' of the iftiʻal into zay and assimilating the zay into it, related by al-Zamakhshari.

﴿Profound wisdom﴾, meaning the Qur'an. It is a substitute for "mā" in His saying: ﴿that which contains a deterrent﴾. It may also be the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: it is wisdom.

﴿But warnings do not avail﴾, when they deny and oppose, as God, Most High, said: ﴿And signs and warnings avail not a people who do not believe﴾ [[See vol. 8, p. 386]]. So "fa-mā" is a negation, meaning the warnings do not avail them. It may also be an interrogative with the meaning of rebuke: "What then do the warnings avail them, when they turn away from them?" And "al-nudhur" may be the plural of "nadhir" (warner) or a verbal noun meaning "warning."

His saying, Most High: ﴿So turn away from them﴾, meaning turn away from them. It was said: this is abrogated by the verse of the sword. It was also said: this is a complete sentence. Then He said: ﴿The day the caller calls﴾. What governs "yawm" (the day) is ﴿they will emerge from the graves﴾, or ﴿humbled﴾, or a hidden verb whose estimate is "remember the day." It was also said: it is with the omission of the particle "fa" and what it governs of the answer to the command, its estimate being: "So turn away from them, for there is for them a day when the caller calls." It was also said: "Turn away from them, O Muhammad, for you have established the proof, and look at them on the day the caller calls." It was also said: meaning turn away from them on the Day of Resurrection and do not ask about them or about their condition, for they will be called ﴿to a terrible thing﴾ and a severe punishment will befall them. This is like when you say: "Do not ask what happened to so-and-so," when you have informed him of a grave matter. It was also said: that is, "and every matter is settled on the day the caller calls." Ibn Kathir read "nukr" with the kaf sukun, and the rest read it with damma; both are dialectal variants, like ʻusr and ʻusur, and shughl and shughul. Its meaning is the dreadful, great matter, which is the Day of Resurrection. The caller is Israfil, peace be upon him. It is narrated from Mujahid and Qatadah that they read "ila shay'in nukira" with kasra on the kaf and fatha on the ra', as a passive verb.

﴿Their eyes humbled﴾. Humility in the eye is submission and abasement, and humility is attributed to the eyes because the trace of honour and humiliation becomes apparent in the human gaze. Allah, Most High, said: ﴿Their eyes cast down﴾ [[See vol. 19, p. 194]] and He said: ﴿humbled from abasement, they glance from a furtive glance﴾ [[See vol. 15, p. 45]]. It is said: khasha'a and ikhtasha'a, meaning he became abased. Khasha'a bi-basarihi means he lowered it. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Abu 'Amr read "khashi'an" with an alif. For active participles, when they precede a plural, both the singular and the feminine are permitted, as in "khashi'an abṣāruhum" and "khashi'atan abṣāruhum" [[See vol. 18, p. 248]], and the plural is also permitted, as in "khushshaʻan abṣāruhum." The poet said (it is al-Harith ibn Daws al-Iyadi, and it is also attributed to Abu Dawud al-Iyadi):

And young men whose faces are handsome,
from Iyad ibn Nizar ibn Ma'ad.

**(Khushshaʿan)** is the plural of *khāshiʿ* (humbled, lowered). It is in the accusative because it is a *ḥāl* (circumstantial qualifier, describing the state of the subject at the time of the action) of the *hāʾ* and *mīm* in **(ʿanhum)**. On this reading, it is wrong to pause at **(ʿanhum)**. It is also permissible for it to be a *ḥāl* of the pronoun in **(yakhrujūn)**, in which case one may pause at **(ʿanhum)**. It has also been read as **(khushshaʿun abṣāruhum)**, with *khushshaʿun* as the predicate of the subject *abṣāruhum*. The clause then has an accusative position as a *ḥāl*, as in the line of poetry:

*"I found him: generosity and nobility are present with him."*

**(Yakhrujūna min al-ajdāth)**: *al-ajdāth* means the graves, singular *jadath*.

**(Ka-annahum jarādun muntashir, muhṭiʿīna ilā al-dāʿ)**: "As if they were scattered locusts, hastening toward the caller." In another place He says: **(Yawma yakūnu al-nāsu ka-al-farāshi al-mabthūth)** ("The day when people will be like scattered moths"). [Cf. vol. 20, p. 165.] These are two descriptions at two different times. The first is at the moment of emerging from the graves: they come out in terror, not knowing where to head, so some of them collide with others. At that time they are like scattered moths, some of them in others, with no direction toward which they aim. The second is when they hear the caller: then they head toward him and become like scattered locusts, since locusts have a direction they aim for.

**(Muhṭiʿīn)** means hastening (*musriʿīn*), as Abu ʿUbayda said. From this is the poet's line:

*"In Tigris is their dwelling, and indeed I see them / in Tigris, hastening toward the sound."*

al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: approaching (*muqbilīn*). Qatada said: intending (*ʿāmidīn*). Ibn ʿAbbas said: looking (*nāẓirīn*). ʿIkrima said: opening their ears toward the sound (*fātiḥīna ādhānahum ilā al-ṣawt*). The meanings are close. It is said: *haṭaʿa al-rajul yahṭaʿu huṭūʿan*, when a man turns toward a thing with his gaze and does not turn away from it; and *ahṭaʿa* means he stretched his neck and lowered his head. The poet said [the speaker is Tubbaʿ]:

*"Nimr ibn Saʿd made me his servant, though I see / that Nimr ibn Saʿd is obedient to me and hastening."*

A camel described as *muhṭiʿ* has an innate downward inclination in its neck. *Ahṭaʿa fī ʿadwihi* means he hastened in his running.

**(Yaqūlu al-kāfirūn hādhā yawmun ʿasir)**: "The disbelievers will say, 'This is a difficult day,'" meaning the Day of Resurrection, because of the hardship they will suffer on it.

Stand up, sons of my mother, and rest your riding beasts,
for I am inclined to a tribe other than you.
The needs have been fulfilled while the night is moonlit,
and the saddles and riding beasts have been tightened for the journey.

When they turned their backs with a clamour among them,
a caller called us at the splitting of dawn.

until its twisted strength became firm upon a rope,
resolute in its determination, neither weak nor feeble.

A poet (the verse is by Imru' al-Qays, whose first hemistich is: "Verily the world is nights and days") said:

and nothing upright remains lasting,

﴿And they denied﴾ our Prophet ﴿and followed their desires﴾, meaning their misguidance and their choices.

It may also be nominative by conjunction with "the Hour," the meaning being: "The Hour has drawn near and every matter is settled," that is, the settling of affairs on the Day of Resurrection has drawn near. Whoever reads it nominative makes it the predicate of "kull."

So he became one whose pursuit of the courtesans
was restrained from his desire by restraint.

It was also read as "muzzajar," by changing the ta' of the iftiʻal into zay and assimilating the zay into it, related by al-Zamakhshari.

﴿Profound wisdom﴾, meaning the Qur'an. It is a substitute for "mā" in His saying: ﴿that which contains a deterrent﴾. It may also be the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: it is wisdom.

﴿But warnings do not avail﴾, when they deny and oppose, as God, Most High, said: ﴿And signs and warnings avail not a people who do not believe﴾ [[See vol. 8, p. 386]]. Abu 'Isa al-Tirmidhi said: this is a hasan sahih hadith. The wording of al-Bukhari from Anas is: "The moon split into two parts."

That is, the approach of the Hour and the splitting of the moon have drawn near, and when the Hour comes, the sky will split along with what is in it, including the moon and others. Al-Mawardi mentioned that this is the view of the majority, and said: because when it splits, no one will fail to see it, since it is a sign, and people are equal regarding signs. Al-Hasan said: "The Hour has drawn near" means that when it comes, the moon will split after the second blast.

It was also said: ﴿and the moon has split﴾ means the matter became clear and manifest, and the Arabs use the moon as a metaphor for what is clear. A poet said:

for I am inclined to a tribe other than you.
The needs have been fulfilled while the night is moonlit,
and the saddles and riding beasts have been tightened for the journey.

It was also said: the splitting of the moon is the splitting of darkness from it by its rising within it, just as dawn is called "falq" (daybreak) because darkness splits away from it. Its emergence is sometimes expressed by "splitting," as al-Nabighah said:

a caller called us at the splitting of dawn.

Stand up, sons of my mother, and rest your riding beasts,
for I am inclined to a tribe other than you.
The needs have been fulfilled while the night is moonlit,
and the saddles and riding beasts have been tightened for the journey.

When they turned their backs with a clamour among them,

resolute in its determination, neither weak nor feeble.

and nothing upright remains lasting,

So he became one whose pursuit of the courtesans
was restrained from his desire by restraint.

And young men whose faces are handsome,
from Iyad ibn Nizar ibn Ma'ad.

*"I found him: generosity and nobility are present with him."*

**(Yakhrujūna min al-ajdāth)**: *al-ajdāth* means the graves, singular *jadath*.

**(Ka-annahum jarādun muntashir, muhṭiʿīna ilā al-dāʿ)**: "As if they were scattered locusts, hastening toward the caller." In another place He says: **(Yawma yakūnu al-nāsu ka-al-farāshi al-mabthūth)** ("The day when people will be like scattered moths"). [Cf. vol. 20, p. 165.] These are two descriptions at two different times. The first is at the moment of emerging from the graves: they come out in terror, not knowing where to head, so some of them collide with others. At that time they are like scattered moths, some of them in others, with no direction toward which they aim. The second is when they hear the caller: then they head toward him and become like scattered locusts, since locusts have a direction they aim for.

**(Muhṭiʿīn)** means hastening (*musriʿīn*), as Abu ʿUbayda said. From this is the poet's line:

*"In Tigris is their dwelling, and indeed I see them / in Tigris, hastening toward the sound."*

al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: approaching (*muqbilīn*). Qatada said: intending (*ʿāmidīn*). Ibn ʿAbbas said: looking (*nāẓirīn*). ʿIkrima said: opening their ears toward the sound (*fātiḥīna ādhānahum ilā al-ṣawt*). The meanings are close. It is said: *haṭaʿa al-rajul yahṭaʿu huṭūʿan*, when a man turns toward a thing with his gaze and does not turn away from it; and *ahṭaʿa* means he stretched his neck and lowered his head. The poet said [the speaker is Tubbaʿ]:

*"Nimr ibn Saʿd made me his servant, though I see / that Nimr ibn Saʿd is obedient to me and hastening."*

A camel described as *muhṭiʿ* has an innate downward inclination in its neck. *Ahṭaʿa fī ʿadwihi* means he hastened in his running.

But this is not sound, as will come. It has fifty-five verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.
In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

It has also been read as **(khushshaʿun abṣāruhum)**, with *khushshaʿun* as the predicate of the subject *abṣāruhum*. The clause then has an accusative position as a *ḥāl*, as in the line of poetry:

*"I found him: generosity and nobility are present with him."*

**(Yakhrujūna min al-ajdāth)**: *al-ajdāth* means the graves, singular *jadath*.

**(Ka-annahum jarādun muntashir, muhṭiʿīna ilā al-dāʿ)**: "As if they were scattered locusts, hastening toward the caller." In another place He says: **(Yawma yakūnu al-nāsu ka-al-farāshi al-mabthūth)** ("The day when people will be like scattered moths"). [Cf. vol. 20, p. 165.] These are two descriptions at two different times. The first is at the moment of emerging from the graves: they come out in terror, not knowing where to head, so some of them collide with others. At that time they are like scattered moths, some of them in others, with no direction toward which they aim. The second is when they hear the caller: then they head toward him and become like scattered locusts, since locusts have a direction they aim for.

**(Muhṭiʿīn)** means hastening (*musriʿīn*), as Abu ʿUbayda said. From this is the poet's line:

*"In Tigris is their dwelling, and indeed I see them / in Tigris, hastening toward the sound."*

al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: approaching (*muqbilīn*). Qatada said: intending (*ʿāmidīn*). Ibn ʿAbbas said: looking (*nāẓirīn*). ʿIkrima said: opening their ears toward the sound (*fātiḥīna ādhānahum ilā al-ṣawt*). The meanings are close. It is said: *haṭaʿa al-rajul yahṭaʿu huṭūʿan*, when a man turns toward a thing with his gaze and does not turn away from it; and *ahṭaʿa* means he stretched his neck and lowered his head. The poet said [the speaker is Tubbaʿ]:

*"Nimr ibn Saʿd made me his servant, though I see / that Nimr ibn Saʿd is obedient to me and hastening."*

A camel described as *muhṭiʿ* has an innate downward inclination in its neck. *Ahṭaʿa fī ʿadwihi* means he hastened in his running.

**(Yaqūlu al-kāfirūn hādhā yawmun ʿasir)**: "The disbelievers will say, 'This is a difficult day,'" meaning the Day of Resurrection, because of the hardship they will suffer on it.

Surah al-Qamar is entirely Meccan according to the majority of scholars. Muqatil said: except for three verses, from His Most High saying: ﴿Or do they say, "We are a united, victorious company"?﴾ up to His saying: ﴿And the Hour is more calamitous and more bitter﴾. But this is not sound, as will come. It has fifty-five verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.
In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿The Hour has drawn near, and the moon has split.﴾ ﴿And if they see a sign, they turn away and say, "Continuous magic."﴾ ﴿They denied and followed their desires, and every matter is settled.﴾ ﴿And there has certainly come to them of the news that which contains a deterrent.﴾ ﴿Profound wisdom, but warnings do not avail.﴾ ﴿So turn away from them. The day the caller calls to a terrible thing.﴾ ﴿Their eyes humbled, they will emerge from the graves as if they were scattered locusts,﴾ ﴿hastening toward the caller. The disbelievers will say, "This is a hard day."﴾

His saying, Most High: ﴿The Hour has drawn near, and the moon has split.﴾ "Has drawn near" means it has come close, like ﴿The Imminent has drawn near﴾ [[See p. 122 of this part.]] (as we have explained). It is near relative to what has passed, because most of the world has already passed, as Qatadah narrated from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave a sermon when the sun was about to set, and said: "What remains of your world compared to what has passed is only like what remains of this day compared to what has passed." And we do not see of the sun except a little. Ka'b and Wahb said: the world is six thousand years. Wahb said: five thousand and six hundred years have already passed of it. Al-Nahhas mentioned this.

Then He said, Most High: ﴿and the moon has split﴾, meaning "and the moon has already split." Hudhayfah read it this way: "The Hour has drawn near, and the moon has indeed split," with the addition of "qad." The majority of scholars hold this view, and it is established in Sahih al-Bukhari and others from the hadiths of Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Umar, Anas, Jubayr ibn Mut'im and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them. It is narrated from Anas that he said: The people of Makkah asked the Prophet (ﷺ) for a sign, so the moon split in Makkah twice, and this was revealed: ﴿The Hour has drawn near, and the moon has split﴾ up to His saying: ﴿continuous magic﴾, meaning passing away. Abu 'Isa al-Tirmidhi said: this is a hasan sahih hadith. The wording of al-Bukhari from Anas is: "The moon split into two parts."

Some people said: the splitting of the moon has not yet occurred; it is awaited. That is, the approach of the Hour and the splitting of the moon have drawn near, and when the Hour comes, the sky will split along with what is in it, including the moon and others. Al-Qushayri also said this. Al-Mawardi mentioned that this is the view of the majority, and said: because when it splits, no one will fail to see it, since it is a sign, and people are equal regarding signs. Al-Hasan said: "The Hour has drawn near" means that when it comes, the moon will split after the second blast.

It was also said: ﴿and the moon has split﴾ means the matter became clear and manifest, and the Arabs use the moon as a metaphor for what is clear. A poet said:

Stand up, sons of my mother, and rest your riding beasts,
for I am inclined to a tribe other than you.
The needs have been fulfilled while the night is moonlit,
and the saddles and riding beasts have been tightened for the journey.

It was also said: the splitting of the moon is the splitting of darkness from it by its rising within it, just as dawn is called "falq" (daybreak) because darkness splits away from it. Its emergence is sometimes expressed by "splitting," as al-Nabighah said:

When they turned their backs with a clamour among them,
a caller called us at the splitting of dawn.

I say: It has been established by the transmission of trustworthy individual narrators that the moon split in Makkah, and this is the apparent meaning of the revelation. It does not follow that people must be equal in witnessing it, because it was a nocturnal sign, and it occurred at the request of the Prophet (ﷺ) to Allah, Most High, at the time of the challenge. It is narrated that Hamzah ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, when he embraced Islam out of anger at Abu Jahl's insulting of the Messenger (ﷺ), asked to be shown a sign by which his certainty in his faith would increase. It has already been mentioned in the Sahih that the people of Makkah were the ones who asked and demanded to be shown a sign, so he showed them the splitting of the moon into two halves, as in the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud and others. It is narrated from Hudhayfah that he gave a sermon in al-Mada'in and then said: "Indeed the Hour has drawn near, and the moon has split in the time of your Prophet (ﷺ)." It has also been said that it is by inversion of order, its meaning being "the moon split and the Hour drew near," as Ibn Kaysan said. It has already been mentioned from al-Farra' that when two verbs are close in meaning, you may place one before the other, at His saying: ﴿Then he drew near and descended﴾ [[See p. 89 of this part.]].

His saying, Most High: ﴿And if they see a sign, they turn away﴾. This indicates that they saw the splitting of the moon. Ibn 'Abbas said: The polytheists gathered before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "If you are truthful, split the moon for us into two parts, half over Abu Qubays and half over Qu'aiqi'an." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to them: "If I do it, will you believe?" They said: "Yes." It was the night of Badr. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked his Lord to give him what they had said, and the moon split into two parts, while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called out to the polytheists: "O so-and-so, O so-and-so, bear witness!" In the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud: the moon split in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and Quraysh said: "This is from the magic of Ibn Abi Kabshah. He has bewitched you, so ask the travellers." They asked them, and they said: "We have seen the moon split." Then this was revealed: ﴿The Hour has drawn near, and the moon has split. And if they see a sign, they turn away﴾, meaning: if they see a sign indicating the truthfulness of Muhammad (ﷺ), they turn away from faith. ﴿And say, "Continuous magic"﴾, meaning passing away, from their saying: "The thing passed and continued" when it went away. This was said by Anas, Qatadah, Mujahid, al-Farra', al-Kisa'i and Abu 'Ubaydah, and al-Nahhas preferred it. Abu al-'Aliyah and al-Dahhak said: firm, strong, intense, and it is from "mirrah," which means strength. As Laqit said:

until its twisted strength became firm upon a rope,
resolute in its determination, neither weak nor feeble.

Al-Akhfash said: it is derived from "imrar al-habl," which means the intensity of twisting a rope. It was also said: its meaning is "bitter," from "marārah" (bitterness). One says: amarra al-shay' (the thing became bitter), and likewise marra al-shay' (with fatha) became bitter, so it is murr; and others caused it to be bitter (amarrahu and marrahu). Al-Rabi' said: continuous, effective. Yamani said: passing. Abu 'Ubaydah said: false. It was also said: lasting. A poet (the verse is by Imru' al-Qays, whose first hemistich is: "Verily the world is nights and days") said:

and nothing upright remains lasting,

meaning, does not last. It was also said: some of it resembles other parts, meaning the actions of Muhammad have continued in this manner, so he brings nothing that has a true reality; rather, all of it is imagination. It was also said: its meaning is that it has passed from the earth to the sky.

﴿And they denied﴾ our Prophet ﴿and followed their desires﴾, meaning their misguidance and their choices.

﴿And every matter is settled﴾, meaning it settles with every doer for what he did: the good settles with its people in Paradise, and the evil settles with its people in Hellfire. Shaybah read "mustaqarr" with a fatha on the qaf, meaning every thing has a time in which it occurs without advance or delay. It is narrated from Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' "wa kullu amrin mustaqarrin" with kasra on the qaf and the ra', making it an adjective of "amr," and "kull" in this case may be nominative as a subject with an omitted predicate, as if he said: "And every matter is settled in the Mother of the Book, existing." It may also be nominative by conjunction with "the Hour," the meaning being: "The Hour has drawn near and every matter is settled," that is, the settling of affairs on the Day of Resurrection has drawn near. Whoever reads it nominative makes it the predicate of "kull."

﴿And there has certainly come to them of the news﴾, meaning from some of the news. He, glorified be He, mentioned of it what He knew they needed, and in which there is healing for them. There were matters beyond this, but He related to us what He knew we need, and remained silent about the rest. This is His saying: ﴿And there has certainly come to them of the news﴾, meaning there came to these disbelievers some of the news of the earlier nations ﴿that which contains a deterrent﴾, meaning what would restrain them from disbelief had they accepted it. Its original form is "muztajar," then the taʼ was changed to dal, because ta' is a voiceless letter and zay is a voiced letter, so the ta' was replaced by a dal which agrees with it in articulation point and agrees with the zay in voicing. "Muzdajar" is from "zajr," which means restraint; one says: zajarahu and izdajarahu, so he was restrained and refrained (infazara and izdajara), and I restrained him so he was restrained (zajartuhu fa-infazara), meaning I held him back so he held back, as the poet said:

So he became one whose pursuit of the courtesans
was restrained from his desire by restraint.

It was also read as "muzzajar," by changing the ta' of the iftiʻal into zay and assimilating the zay into it, related by al-Zamakhshari.

﴿Profound wisdom﴾, meaning the Qur'an. It is a substitute for "mā" in His saying: ﴿that which contains a deterrent﴾. It may also be the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: it is wisdom.

﴿But warnings do not avail﴾, when they deny and oppose, as God, Most High, said: ﴿And signs and warnings avail not a people who do not believe﴾ [[See vol. 8, p. 386]]. So "fa-mā" is a negation, meaning the warnings do not avail them. It may also be an interrogative with the meaning of rebuke: "What then do the warnings avail them, when they turn away from them?" And "al-nudhur" may be the plural of "nadhir" (warner) or a verbal noun meaning "warning."

His saying, Most High: ﴿So turn away from them﴾, meaning turn away from them. It was said: this is abrogated by the verse of the sword. It was also said: this is a complete sentence. Then He said: ﴿The day the caller calls﴾. What governs "yawm" (the day) is ﴿they will emerge from the graves﴾, or ﴿humbled﴾, or a hidden verb whose estimate is "remember the day." It was also said: it is with the omission of the particle "fa" and what it governs of the answer to the command, its estimate being: "So turn away from them, for there is for them a day when the caller calls." It was also said: "Turn away from them, O Muhammad, for you have established the proof, and look at them on the day the caller calls." It was also said: meaning turn away from them on the Day of Resurrection and do not ask about them or about their condition, for they will be called ﴿to a terrible thing﴾ and a severe punishment will befall them. This is like when you say: "Do not ask what happened to so-and-so," when you have informed him of a grave matter. It was also said: that is, "and every matter is settled on the day the caller calls." Ibn Kathir read "nukr" with the kaf sukun, and the rest read it with damma; both are dialectal variants, like ʻusr and ʻusur, and shughl and shughul. Its meaning is the dreadful, great matter, which is the Day of Resurrection. The caller is Israfil, peace be upon him. It is narrated from Mujahid and Qatadah that they read "ila shay'in nukira" with kasra on the kaf and fatha on the ra', as a passive verb.

﴿Their eyes humbled﴾. Humility in the eye is submission and abasement, and humility is attributed to the eyes because the trace of honour and humiliation becomes apparent in the human gaze. Allah, Most High, said: ﴿Their eyes cast down﴾ [[See vol. 19, p. 194]] and He said: ﴿humbled from abasement, they glance from a furtive glance﴾ [[See vol. 15, p. 45]]. It is said: khasha'a and ikhtasha'a, meaning he became abased. Khasha'a bi-basarihi means he lowered it. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Abu 'Amr read "khashi'an" with an alif. For active participles, when they precede a plural, both the singular and the feminine are permitted, as in "khashi'an abṣāruhum" and "khashi'atan abṣāruhum" [[See vol. 18, p. 248]], and the plural is also permitted, as in "khushshaʻan abṣāruhum." The poet said (it is al-Harith ibn Daws al-Iyadi, and it is also attributed to Abu Dawud al-Iyadi):

And young men whose faces are handsome,
from Iyad ibn Nizar ibn Ma'ad.

**(Khushshaʿan)** is the plural of *khāshiʿ* (humbled, lowered). It is in the accusative because it is a *ḥāl* (circumstantial qualifier, describing the state of the subject at the time of the action) of the *hāʾ* and *mīm* in **(ʿanhum)**. On this reading, it is wrong to pause at **(ʿanhum)**. It is also permissible for it to be a *ḥāl* of the pronoun in **(yakhrujūn)**, in which case one may pause at **(ʿanhum)**. It has also been read as **(khushshaʿun abṣāruhum)**, with *khushshaʿun* as the predicate of the subject *abṣāruhum*. The clause then has an accusative position as a *ḥāl*, as in the line of poetry:

*"I found him: generosity and nobility are present with him."*

**(Yakhrujūna min al-ajdāth)**: *al-ajdāth* means the graves, singular *jadath*.

**(Ka-annahum jarādun muntashir, muhṭiʿīna ilā al-dāʿ)**: "As if they were scattered locusts, hastening toward the caller." In another place He says: **(Yawma yakūnu al-nāsu ka-al-farāshi al-mabthūth)** ("The day when people will be like scattered moths"). [Cf. vol. 20, p. 165.] These are two descriptions at two different times. The first is at the moment of emerging from the graves: they come out in terror, not knowing where to head, so some of them collide with others. At that time they are like scattered moths, some of them in others, with no direction toward which they aim. The second is when they hear the caller: then they head toward him and become like scattered locusts, since locusts have a direction they aim for.

**(Muhṭiʿīn)** means hastening (*musriʿīn*), as Abu ʿUbayda said. From this is the poet's line:

*"In Tigris is their dwelling, and indeed I see them / in Tigris, hastening toward the sound."*

al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: approaching (*muqbilīn*). Qatada said: intending (*ʿāmidīn*). Ibn ʿAbbas said: looking (*nāẓirīn*). ʿIkrima said: opening their ears toward the sound (*fātiḥīna ādhānahum ilā al-ṣawt*). The meanings are close. It is said: *haṭaʿa al-rajul yahṭaʿu huṭūʿan*, when a man turns toward a thing with his gaze and does not turn away from it; and *ahṭaʿa* means he stretched his neck and lowered his head. The poet said [the speaker is Tubbaʿ]:

*"Nimr ibn Saʿd made me his servant, though I see / that Nimr ibn Saʿd is obedient to me and hastening."*

A camel described as *muhṭiʿ* has an innate downward inclination in its neck. *Ahṭaʿa fī ʿadwihi* means he hastened in his running.

**(Yaqūlu al-kāfirūn hādhā yawmun ʿasir)**: "The disbelievers will say, 'This is a difficult day,'" meaning the Day of Resurrection, because of the hardship they will suffer on it.

﴿Before them the people of Noah denied﴾. He mentions some events of past nations to console the Prophet ﷺ and comfort him.

(Before them) means before your people.

(So they denied Our servant) meaning Noah. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, what is the meaning of His words "so they denied" after His words "denied"? I say: its meaning is that they denied, and then they denied Our servant, that is, they denied him with denial following denial. Whenever one denying generation passed away, another denying generation followed it. Or, the people of Noah denied the messengers, and then they denied Our servant. That is, since they were deniers of the messengers and rejecters of prophethood altogether, they denied Noah because he was one of the messengers.

(And they said, "He is mad") meaning he is mad. (And he was rebuked) meaning he was restrained from claiming prophethood by insults and threats of killing. It has been said that He said "wa-zdujira" (and he was rebuked) in the passive form without naming the agent because it is the end of the verse (ra's ayah, the verse-final position).

(So he called upon his Lord) meaning Noah then called down (a curse) upon them and said: "My Lord, (I am overpowered) meaning they have overcome me through their rebelliousness, (so help) meaning so help me." It has been said that the prophets did not call down destruction upon their peoples except with permission from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for that.

(So We opened the gates of heaven) meaning We answered his supplication, commanded him to build the ark, and opened the gates of heaven (with water pouring down) meaning abundant, as al-Suddi said. The poet said:

"My eyes, pour forth tears in abundance
over the best of those who dwell in Ma'add and the settled."

It has also been said that it means flowing and gushing. From this is the saying of Imru' al-Qays describing a rain cloud:
"The dawn wind milked it at the time of the return, then it went off,
in it a downpour of southern rain pouring forth."
[[Rāḥ: he returned in the afternoon, as if the rain had been at the beginning of the day and then returned at its end. Tamrīhi: milks it, originally from marā the udder, which means stroking it to make it flow. Al-shu'ubūb: a single burst of rain. He specified the eastern wind (al-ṣabā) because they receive rain by it.]]

Al-hamr means pouring, and water and tears "yahmir" (pour) "hamran." It also means to speak much and quickly, and "hamara lahu min malihi" means he gave him from his wealth. Ibn 'Abbas said: "So We opened the gates of heaven with water pouring down" without clouds, which did not cease for forty days. Ibn 'Amir and Ya'qub recited "fa-fattahna" (with doubled consonant) for intensification. The rest recited "fafatahna" with a single consonant. Then it has been said: it is the opening of its locks and the broadness of its passages. It has been said: it is the Milky Way, which is the outlet of the heaven, and from it the heaven was opened with water pouring down, as 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said.

(And We caused the earth to burst forth with springs) 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr said: Allah revealed to the earth that it should bring forth its water, and it burst forth with springs. A spring lagged behind, so He became angry with it and made its water bitter and salty until the Day of Resurrection.

(And the waters met) meaning the water of the sky and the water of the earth (for a matter already decreed) meaning to a measure in which neither of them exceeded the other. Ibn Qutayba related this, that is, the water of the sky and the earth were equal. It has been said: "decreed" means "decided against them." Qatada said: He decreed for them, when they disbelieved, that they would drown. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: The provisions were before the bodies, and the decree was before the trial, and he recited this verse. And he said: "the waters met," and meeting only occurs between two or more, because water can be both a collective noun and a singular. It has been said: because when the two came together they became one water. Al-Jahdari recited "al-ma'ani" (the two waters). Al-Hasan recited "al-mawani" (the two waters), which are contrary to the written consonantal text. Al-Qushayri said: In some codices it is "al-mawani," which is the dialect of Tayy. It has been said: the water of the sky was cold like snow, and the water of the earth was hot like boiling water.

(And We carried him upon a vessel of planks) meaning upon a ship having planks.

(And nails) Qatada said: meaning the nails with which the ship was fastened (dusira), that is, tightened. This was also said by al-Qurazi, Ibn Zayd and Ibn Jubayr, and al-Walibi related it from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Hasan, Shahr ibn Hawshab and 'Ikrima said: it is the prow of the ship, which strikes the waves, and it was named so because it pushes (tadsuru) the water, that is, drives it away. The "dasr" is pushing and thrusting. al-'Awfi related from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "al-dasr" is the chest (kulkul) of the ship.
[[Al-kulkul: the chest.]]

Al-Layth said: al-disar is a thread of palm fiber with which the planks of the ship are tied. In al-Sihah: al-disar is the singular of al-dusur, and they are cords with which the planks of the ship are tied. It is said they are nails. Allah the Exalted said: "upon a vessel of planks and nails." Dusr is also like 'usr and 'usur. Al-dasr is pushing. Ibn 'Abbas said regarding the ambergris: it is something the sea pushes out, that is, drives away. He "dasarahu" with a spear, and a man is "midsar" (one who pushes hard).

(Sailing under Our eyes) meaning in Our sight. It has been said: by Our command. It has been said: under Our protection and care. This has already passed in (Hud) [[See vol. 9 p. 30.]]. From this is the saying of people to one departing: "the eye of Allah be upon you," meaning His protection and care. It has been said: by Our revelation. It has been said: meaning by the springs gushing from the earth. It has been said: by the eyes of Our friends among the angels who are charged with guarding it. Everything Allah the Exalted created may be attributed to Him. It has been said: meaning they sail among Our friends, as in the report: "One of Our eyes fell ill, so it was not visited."

(As a recompense for one who had been disbelieved) meaning We made that a reward and recompense for Noah for his patience over the harm of his people, and he was the one disbelieved. So the "li" in "liman" is the "li" of the object of purpose. It has also been said: "kufira" means denied, so "liman" refers to Noah. It has been said: it refers to Allah, and "al-jaza'" means punishment, meaning a punishment for their disbelief in Allah the Exalted. Yazid ibn Ruman, Qatada, Mujahid and Humayd recited "jaza'an liman kana kufira" with a fatha on the kaf and fa, meaning the drowning was a recompense and punishment for one who disbelieved in Allah. None escaped the drowning except 'Uj ibn 'Unuq [[Ibn 'Unuq is the well-known form, and the one preferred by the author of al-Qamus is Ibn 'Awq, not 'Unuq.]], the water reached only his waist. The cause of his salvation was that Noah needed a teak beam for building the ship, and he could not carry it, so 'Uj carried that beam to him from Syria, so Allah thanked him for that and saved him from drowning.

(And We have left it as a sign) meaning this deed as a lesson. It has been said: he meant the ship, which He left as a sign for those after the people of Noah to take warning from, so that they would not deny the messengers. Qatada said: Allah preserved it at Baqirdan in the land of al-Jazira as a lesson and sign, until the first of this community saw it, and how many ships came after it and became ashes.

(So is there any who will remember?) meaning one who is admonished and fearful. Its origin is "mudhtakir" (the form ifta'ala from dhikr), but it was heavy on the tongue, so the ta' was changed into a dal to harmonize with the dhal in voicing, and the dhal was assimilated into it.

(So how was My punishment and warning?) i.e., My warning. Al-Farra' said: "al-indhar" and "al-nadhr" are both verbal nouns. It has been said: "nudhur" is the plural of "nadhir," and "nadhir" in the sense of "indhar" is like "nakir" in the sense of "inkar."

(And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for remembrance) meaning We made it easy to memorize and helped whoever wishes to memorize it. So is there anyone who seeks to memorize it so that he may be helped to do so? It may also mean: We prepared it for remembrance, derived from "yassara his she-camel for travel," when he saddled it, and "yassara his horse for battle" when he bridled it and put on its bit. He said:

"I stood up to it with the bridle, making it ready;
there, what I used to do will repay me."

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: There is no book of Allah that can be read entirely by heart except the Qur'an. Others said: This was not so for the Children of Israel, who did not read the Torah except by looking at it, except Moses, Aaron, Joshua son of Nun and 'Uzayr, peace be upon them. That is, since they were deniers of the messengers and rejecters of prophethood altogether, they denied Noah because he was one of the messengers.

It has been said that He said "wa-zdujira" (and he was rebuked) in the passive form without naming the agent because it is the end of the verse (ra's ayah, the verse-final position).

(So he called upon his Lord) meaning Noah then called down (a curse) upon them and said: "My Lord, (I am overpowered) meaning they have overcome me through their rebelliousness, (so help) meaning so help me." It has been said that the prophets did not call down destruction upon their peoples except with permission from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for that.

(So We opened the gates of heaven) meaning We answered his supplication, commanded him to build the ark, and opened the gates of heaven (with water pouring down) meaning abundant, as al-Suddi said. The poet said:

"My eyes, pour forth tears in abundance
over the best of those who dwell in Ma'add and the settled."

It has also been said that it means flowing and gushing. From this is the saying of Imru' al-Qays describing a rain cloud:
"The dawn wind milked it at the time of the return, then it went off,
in it a downpour of southern rain pouring forth."
[[Rāḥ: he returned in the afternoon, as if the rain had been at the beginning of the day and then returned at its end. Tamrīhi: milks it, originally from marā the udder, which means stroking it to make it flow. Al-shu'ubūb: a single burst of rain. He specified the eastern wind (al-ṣabā) because they receive rain by it.]]

Ibn 'Amir and Ya'qub recited "fa-fattahna" (with doubled consonant) for intensification. The rest recited "fafatahna" with a single consonant. Then it has been said: it is the opening of its locks and the broadness of its passages. It has been said: it is the Milky Way, which is the outlet of the heaven, and from it the heaven was opened with water pouring down, as 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said.

(And We caused the earth to burst forth with springs) 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr said: Allah revealed to the earth that it should bring forth its water, and it burst forth with springs. A spring lagged behind, so He became angry with it and made its water bitter and salty until the Day of Resurrection.

(And the waters met) meaning the water of the sky and the water of the earth (for a matter already decreed) meaning to a measure in which neither of them exceeded the other. Ibn Qutayba related this, that is, the water of the sky and the earth were equal. It has been said: "decreed" means "decided against them." Qatada said: He decreed for them, when they disbelieved, that they would drown. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: The provisions were before the bodies, and the decree was before the trial, and he recited this verse. And he said: "the waters met," and meeting only occurs between two or more, because water can be both a collective noun and a singular. It has been said: because when the two came together they became one water. Al-Jahdari recited "al-ma'ani" (the two waters). Al-Hasan recited "al-mawani" (the two waters), which are contrary to the written consonantal text. Al-Qushayri said: In some codices it is "al-mawani," which is the dialect of Tayy. It has been said: the water of the sky was cold like snow, and the water of the earth was hot like boiling water.

(And We carried him upon a vessel of planks) meaning upon a ship having planks.

(And nails) Qatada said: meaning the nails with which the ship was fastened (dusira), that is, tightened. [[Al-kulkul: the chest.]]

Al-Layth said: al-disar is a thread of palm fiber with which the planks of the ship are tied. In al-Sihah: al-disar is the singular of al-dusur, and they are cords with which the planks of the ship are tied. It is said they are nails. Everything Allah the Exalted created may be attributed to Him. It has been said: meaning they sail among Our friends, as in the report: "One of Our eyes fell ill, so it was not visited."

**Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 54, verses 18–22:**

Allah's words: ﴿كَذَّبَتْ عَادٌ﴾ ("'Ad denied"). They are the people of Hud.

﴿فَكَيْفَ كَانَ عَذَابِي وَنُذُرِ﴾ ("So how was My punishment and My warnings?"). The word *nudhur* (warnings) occurs in this surah in six places, and in all the copies of the Qur'an (*mushaf*, pl. *masahif*) the *ya'* is omitted. Ya'qub reads it with the *ya'* in both pausal and continuous recitation. Warsh reads it with the *ya'* only in continuous recitation. The others omit it. There is no disagreement about omitting the *ya'* in ﴿فَمَا تُغْنِ النُّذُرُ﴾ ("the warnings did not avail") or the *waw* in ﴿يَدْعُ﴾ ("calls"). As for the *ya'* in the first *al-Da'i* (the caller), Ibn Muhaysin, Ya'qub, Humayd and al-Bazzi keep it in both states, Warsh and Abu 'Amr keep it in continuous recitation, and the others omit it. As for the second *al-Da'i*, Ya'qub, Ibn Muhaysin and Ibn Kathir keep it in both states, Abu 'Amr and Nafi' keep it in continuous recitation, and the others omit it.

﴿فَكَيْفَ كَانَ عَذَابِي وَنُذُرِ﴾ ("So how was My punishment and My warnings?"). The word *nudhur* (warnings) occurs in this surah in six places, and in all the copies of the Qur'an (*mushaf*, pl. *masahif*) the *ya'* is omitted. Ya'qub reads it with the *ya'* in both pausal and continuous recitation. Warsh reads it with the *ya'* only in continuous recitation. The others omit it. There is no disagreement about omitting the *ya'* in ﴿فَمَا تُغْنِ النُّذُرُ﴾ ("the warnings did not avail") or the *waw* in ﴿يَدْعُ﴾ ("calls"). As for the *ya'* in the first *al-Da'i* (the caller), Ibn Muhaysin, Ya'qub, Humayd and al-Bazzi keep it in both states, Warsh and Abu 'Amr keep it in continuous recitation, and the others omit it. As for the second *al-Da'i*, Ya'qub, Ibn Muhaysin and Ibn Kathir keep it in both states, Abu 'Amr and Nafi' keep it in continuous recitation, and the others omit it.

﴿إِنَّا أَرْسَلْنَا عَلَيْهِمْ رِيحًا صَرْصَرًا﴾ ("Indeed, We sent upon them a violent wind"). That is, a wind of intense cold, as said by Qatadah and al-Dahhak. It was also said that it was a wind of intense sound. This has already been discussed in *Ha Mim* (al-Sajdah).

﴿فِي يَوْمِ نَحْسٍ مُسْتَمِرٍّ﴾ ("on a day of ill omen, continuing"). That is, on a day that was ill-omened for them. Ibn 'Abbas said: that is, a day by which they used to take omens of misfortune. Al-Zajjaj said: it was said that it was on a Wednesday. Ibn 'Abbas said: it was the last Wednesday of the month, and it destroyed their young and their old. Harun al-A'war read *nahs* with a *kasra* on the *ha'*. The discussion of this has already been given in *Ha Mim* (al-Sajdah), in the words ﴿فِي أَيَّامٍ نَحِسَاتٍ﴾ ("on days of ill omen"). As for ﴿فِي يَوْمِ نَحْسٍ مُسْتَمِرٍّ﴾, it means: a day that is constantly ill-omened, its misfortune persisted over them, and the punishment continued upon them in it until their destruction. It was also said: it continued with them into the fire of Hell. Al-Dahhak said: it was bitter for them. Al-Kisa'i likewise reported that some people said it is from *al-marara* (bitterness); it is said *murra al-shay'* and *amarra*, meaning the thing was like a bitter thing that souls dislike. And He has said ﴿فَذُوقُوا﴾ ("so taste"), and what is tasted may well be bitter. It has also been said that it is from *al-mirrah* in the sense of strength, meaning: on a day of ill omen, continuing, its misfortune firmly established, like a firmly twisted thing whose undoing cannot be borne.

If it is asked: if Wednesday is a day of continuing ill omen, how is supplication answered on it? It has been reported that the Prophet (ﷺ) had his supplication answered on it between noon and the afternoon prayer, and the hadith of Jabir to this effect has already been mentioned in *al-Baqarah*. The answer, and Allah knows best, is what is reported in a narration transmitted by Masruq from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Gabriel came to me and said: Indeed Allah commands you to judge by the oath together with a witness," and he said: "Wednesday is a day of continuing ill omen." It is known that he did not mean that it was ill-omened for the righteous; rather he meant that it was ill-omened for the wicked and the corrupters, just as the ill-omened days mentioned in the Qur'an were ill-omened for the disbelievers of the people of 'Ad, and not for their prophet and the believers among them. If that is so, it is not unlikely that the wrongdoer is given respite from the start of Wednesday until the sun declines. When the day turns its back and has not brought about a return, the supplication of the one wronged against him is answered, so the day becomes ill-omened for the wrongdoer. The supplication of the Prophet (ﷺ) was only against the disbelievers. The words of Jabir in his hadith, "No grave matter had befallen me," point to this. And Allah knows best.

Allah's words: ﴿تَنْزِعُ النَّاسَ كَأَنَّهُمْ أَعْجَازُ نَخْلٍ مُنْقَعِرٍ﴾ ("plucking people up as though they were trunks of uprooted palm trees"). The phrase is in the position of a description of the wind, that is, it uproots them from their places. It was said: it uprooted them from beneath their feet, as a palm is uprooted from its base. Mujahid said: it used to pluck them from the ground and hurl them onto their heads, so their necks would break and their heads would be separated from their bodies. It was also said: it plucks the people from their houses. Muhammad ibn Ka'b reported from his father, who said: the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The wind snatched the people from their graves." It was also said: they dug pits and entered them, and the wind would pluck them out of them and break them, and it left those pits like the roots of palm trees, whose contents had perished, so their places remained uprooted. It is narrated that seven of them dug pits and stood in them in order to turn back the wind. Ibn Ishaq said: when the wind raged, seven men of 'Ad stood up. Six of them were named for us, among the strongest and largest of 'Ad: 'Amr ibn al-Hulayy, al-Harith ibn Shaddad, al-Hilqam, the two sons of Tiqn, and Khalajan ibn Sa'd. They put the women and children into a ravine between two mountains, then lined up at the mouth of the ravine to turn back the wind from those in the ravine of the dependents. But the wind began to throw them down one by one, and a woman of 'Ad said:

Time has taken 'Amr ibn Hulayy and the Hunayyat,
then al-Harith and al-Hilqam, the climber of the high passes,
and the one who blocked the path of the wind in days of calamity.

Al-Tabari said: there is an ellipsis in the speech, and the meaning is: "plucking people and leaving them as though they were trunks of uprooted palm trees." So the *kaf* (as) is in the accusative position governed by the omitted verb. Al-Zajjaj said: the *kaf* is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*hal*), and the meaning is: plucking people, likened to trunks of palm trees. The comparison was said to refer to the pits in which they were. *A'jaz* is the plural of *ajuz*, which is the hindmost part of a thing. The people of 'Ad were described as having great stature, so they were likened to palm trees that have fallen on their faces. He said ﴿أَعْجَازُ نَخْلٍ مُنْقَعِرٍ﴾, using the masculine form because of the word *nakhl* (palm), which is a collective noun that may be treated as masculine or feminine. *Al-Munqa'ir* means uprooted from its base; one says *qa'artu al-shajarah qa'ran*, meaning I uprooted the tree from its base, and it became *inqa'arat*. Al-Kisa'i said: *qa'artu al-bi'r* means I descended until I reached its bottom, and likewise a vessel when I drank what was in it until I reached its bottom. *Aq'artu al-bi'r* means I made a bottom for it. Abu Bakr ibn al-Anbari said: al-Mubarrad was asked in the presence of Isma'il al-Qadi about a thousand questions, and this was among them. It was asked of him: what is the difference between the words of Allah, ﴿وَلِسُلَيْمَانَ الرِّيحَ عَاصِفَةً﴾ ("And to Solomon, the wind, violently blowing"), and ﴿جَاءَتْهَا رِيحٌ عَاصِفٌ﴾ ("there came upon it a violent wind"), and His words ﴿كَأَنَّهُمْ أَعْجَازُ نَخْلٍ خَاوِيَةٍ﴾ ("as though they were trunks of hollow palm trees") and ﴿أَعْجَازُ نَخْلٍ مُنْقَعِرٍ﴾? He said: whatever comes to you from this category, if you wish you may refer it to the wording and use the masculine, or to the meaning and use the feminine. It was also said: *al-nakhl* and *al-nakhil* have the same meaning, and they may be masculine or feminine, as we have mentioned.

﴿فَكَيْفَ كَانَ عَذَابِي وَنُذُرِ. وَلَقَدْ يَسَّرْنَا الْقُرْآنَ لِلذِّكْرِ فَهَلْ مِنْ مُدَّكِرٍ﴾ ("So how was My punishment and My warnings? And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for remembrance, so is there any who will remember?") [previously mentioned].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 54, verses 23–26:

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Thamud denied the warnings.﴾ They were the people of Salih. They denied the messengers and their prophet. Or they denied the signs, which are the warnings. ﴿They said: "Shall we follow a single human being from among us?"﴾ and leave a group behind.

Abu al-Ashhab, Ibn al-Sumayqa' and Abu al-Sammal al-'Adawi read ﴿abasharun﴾ with a nominative ending, and ﴿wahidun﴾ likewise with a nominative ending, being the subject (mubtada') with ﴿nattabi'uhu﴾ as its predicate (khabar). The rest read it with the accusative, meaning: "Shall we follow a human being from among us, a single one, whom we follow?"

Abu al-Sammal [[This is another transmission from Abu al-Sammal, as in Ruh al-Ma'ani and others. In manuscripts B, Z and L it is written "Abu al-Simak" with a kaf, which is not correct.]] read ﴿abasharun﴾ with a nominative ending and ﴿minna wahidan﴾ with an accusative ending. The word ﴿abasharun﴾ is nominative by the implied verb indicated by ﴿a-ulqiya﴾, as if he said: "Is a human being from among us being informed?" As for his saying ﴿wahidan﴾, it may be a circumstantial accusative (hal) from the pronoun in ﴿minna﴾, with the adverbial element as its governing word, the implied meaning being: "Is a human being, existing from among us, alone, being informed?" It may also be a circumstantial accusative from the pronoun in ﴿nattabi'uhu﴾, meaning: "alone, with no one to support him."

﴿Then indeed we would be in error﴾, that is, straying from the right course, ﴿and madness﴾, that is, insanity, from their saying: "a she-camel that is maswurah," meaning that from the intensity of her vigour she is as if crazed. Ibn Abbas mentioned this. A poet describing his she-camel said:

"You think her to be crazed when the journey shakes her, a trot and a pace of the journey, exhausting."

[The dhamil is a type of camel's gait. Abu Ubayd said: when the pace rises slightly above the 'anaq, it is the tazayyud; when it rises above that, it is the dhamil, then the rasim. It is said: dhamala yadhmulu and yadhmilu dhamilan. Al-Asma'i said: no camel travels a day and a night at the dhamil except a Mahri camel. [[Addition from B and H.]] This was said by J.]

Ibn Abbas also said: ﴿su'ur﴾ means punishment, and al-Farra' said likewise. Mujahid said: remoteness from the truth. Al-Suddi said: burning. [[It is Tarafa.]] He said:

"Have you awakened today, or has love for Hirr (a woman's name) stirred you, and of love is a madness ablaze?"

That is, kindled and burning. Abu 'Ubayda said: it is the plural of sa'ir, which is the flame of fire. The crazed camel goes such-and-such a way because of the heat of its frenzy. [[In A, Z, L: al-si'ir.]] The meaning of the verse: then indeed we would be in misery and hardship because of what would be incumbent upon us.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Has the Reminder been cast upon him from among us?﴾, that is, has he been singled out for the message from among the family of Thamud, when among them are those who have more wealth and a better condition? It is an interrogative with the meaning of denial.

﴿Rather, he is a liar, an insolent one﴾, that is, he is not as he claims; he only wants to make himself great and seek arrogance over us without entitlement. Al-Ashar means exultation, arrogance and vigour. It is said: "a horse that is ashir" when it is frisky and energetic. Imru' al-Qays said describing a dog:

"Then there overtakes us a keen, domesticated one, hearing, seeing, eager for the hunt, and unusual in appearance."

[Al-Faghm: one devoted to hunting and eager for it. Dajin: tame for hunting. Fakir: that is, knowing/discerning. It is said nakir: of repulsive form.]

[Al-Alassu: one whose teeth are pressed together.] "Strong-toothed, with curved ribs, a tabu', keen, vigorous, ashir."

It is also said: ﴿ashir﴾ means insolent. Al-Ashar is insolence, the poet said:

"You became insolent by wearing silk brocade, when you wore it, and before, you did not know who conquered the towns."

One becomes ashir with a kasra, yaʼshar ashar, so he is ashir or ashran, and the people are ushara like sakran and sukara. The poet said: [[She is Maiyya bint Dirar al-Dabbi lamenting her brother. "Azhafa al-tu'n abtalaha" means the spear-thrust laid their heroes low. Before the verse:

"You see him on the horses, one in the front, when the blood soaks their flanks."]]:

"And she left wild cattle ushara therein, and the spear-thrust had laid their heroes low."

It is also said: he is one who oversteps to a rank he does not deserve, and the meaning is the same. Ibn Zayd and Abd al-Rahman ibn Hammad said: al-Ashir is the one who does not care what he says. Abu Ja'far and Abu Qilaba read ﴿ashsharu﴾ with a fatha on the shin and tashdid on the ra', meaning "our most insolent and most wicked."

﴿They will know tomorrow﴾, that is, they will see the punishment on the Day of Resurrection, or at the time the punishment descends upon them in this world. Ibn 'Amir and Hamza read it with the ta' (tasta'lamun), as being the words of Salih to them in direct address. The rest read it with the ya' (ya'lamun), as a report from Allah the Exalted to Salih about them. His saying ﴿ghadan﴾ is by approximation, in the customary way of people who say of consequences: "Indeed, with today comes tomorrow." A poet said:

"Death has arrows in it that never miss; whoever is not dead today will die tomorrow."

And al-Tirimmah said:

"Ah, treat me with cure before the wailing of the mourners, and before the agitation of the soul among the ribs.

And before tomorrow, alas for my soul over tomorrow, when my companions depart and I am not departing."

He meant the time of death, not tomorrow itself.

﴿Who is the liar, the insolent one?﴾ Abu Qilaba read al-ashar with a fatha on the shin and tashdid on the ra', coming in the original form. Abu Hatim said: the Arabs hardly speak with al-ashar and al-akhyar except in poetic necessity, like the verse of Ru'ba: "Bilal is the best of people and the son of the best," whereas they say "he is the best of his people," and he is the worst of people. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind﴾ [[See vol. 4, p. 170.]] and He said: ﴿They will know who is worst in position﴾ [[See vol. 11, p. 144.]]. It is also reported from Abu Haywa with a fatha on the shin and a light ra'. It is reported from Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr with a damma on the shin and ra' and light pronunciation. Al-Nahhas said: this is the meaning of al-ashir, and like it is rajul hadhar and hadhir.

(إِنَّا مُرْسِلُوا النَّاقَةِ) ﴿Indeed, We are sending the she-camel﴾, meaning: bringing it out from the rock-face that they asked for. It is related that Salih prayed two rak'ahs and supplicated, and the rock they had specified split open at its side, and out came a pregnant she-camel [wabra'* ].[[In the manuscripts it reads "jarda'" (hairless), but what appears in Qisas al-Anbiya' by al-Tha'labi and other tafsir works is "wabra'" (furry), so we have adopted it.]]

(فِتْنَةً لَهُمْ) ﴿as a trial for them﴾, meaning: as a test. It is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu).

(فَارْتَقِبْهُمْ) ﴿so watch them﴾, meaning: wait and see what they do.

(وَاصْطَبِرْ) ﴿and be patient﴾, meaning: be patient with their harm. The original letter of the ta' in iṣṭabir is a ta', which was changed into a ta' (ṭa') so that it would match the ṣad in being emphatic (iṭbaq).

(وَنَبِّئْهُمْ) ﴿and inform them﴾, meaning: tell them ﴿that the water is to be shared between them﴾, meaning between the people of Thamud and the she-camel: for her there is a day and for them there is a day, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿for her is a drink, and for you is a drink on an appointed day﴾ [[See vol. 13, p. 127.]]. Ibn 'Abbas said: On their day of drinking, the she-camel would not drink any water, and she would give them milk, and they were in comfort. But when it was the she-camel's day, she would drink all the water and leave them nothing. He said "between them" because when the Arabs speak of human beings together with animals, they give precedence to the human beings. Abu al-Zubayr related from Jabir, who said: When we stopped at al-Hijr during the expedition of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to Tabuk, he said: "O people, do not ask for signs such as these. These were the people of Salih, who asked their prophet that Allah send them a she-camel. So Allah, mighty and majestic, sent them the she-camel, and she would come to them from that mountain pass and drink their water on the day of her coming, and they would milk from her as much as they used to drink on the day of her absence." This is the meaning of His words: ﴿and inform them that the water is shared between them﴾.

(كُلُّ شِرْبٍ مُحْتَضَرٌ) ﴿every drinking is attended﴾. Ash-shirb (with a kasra) means one's share of water. There is a proverb: "The last of them is the least in drink," and its origin is in watering camels, because the last of them comes to the water when the trough has already been drained. The meaning of "attended" (muhtadar) is that each one present is entitled to his share: the she-camel comes to the water on her day, and is absent from them on their day. This is what Muqatil said. Mujahid said: The people of Thamud would come to the water on the day of her absence and drink, and they would come to the milk on the day of her coming and milk her.

Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So they called their companion﴾, meaning: by urging him to hamstring her, ﴿and he took it in hand and hamstrung her﴾. The meaning of ta'aṭa is "to take up the action," from the expression 'aṭawtu, meaning "I reached out," and from it is the verse of Hassan:

"Both of them are the milkers of the juice, so hand me
a cup, the more relaxing of the two for the joints."

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: He lay in wait for her at the foot of a tree on her path and shot her with an arrow, which struck the muscle of her leg. Then he rushed at her with a sword and cut her hamstring, and she fell and cried out in a single cry, and her young one slid from her belly. Then he slaughtered her, and her young one ran off until it reached a rock at the top of a mountain, where it cried out and then took refuge in it. Then Salih, peace be upon him, came to them, and when he saw that the she-camel had been hamstrung, he wept and said: "You have violated the sanctity of Allah, so rejoice in the punishment of Allah." The explanation of this meaning has already passed in (al-A'raf) [[See vol. 7, p. 241.]]. Ibn 'Abbas said: The one who hamstrung her was reddish, bluish, reddish-white, with a shrunken face and a short neck. It is said that his name was Qudar ibn Salif. Al-Afwah al-Awdi said:

"Before him, or after him, like Qudar, when peoples followed him
into error, and they perished."

The Arabs call the butcher "Qaddar," in likeness to Miqdar ibn Salif, the ill-omened one of the family of Thamud. Muhalhil said:

"We strike their heads with swords,
striking like the butcher striking the feast-offering of the travelers."
[Qaddar: the butcher. Naqi'a: what is slaughtered for hospitality. Qidam: those returning from a journey, plural of qadim. It is also said that qidam means a king. Another reading is: "We strike their heads with sharp swords."]

Zuhayr also mentioned him, saying:

"She will bring forth for you boys, all of them ill-omened,
like the Red One of 'Ad; then she will suckle and wean."
[Tuntij lakum means war. "Ghilman ashʼam" means "boys of ill omen," or "all of them in ill omen like the Red One of 'Ad." "Thumma turdi'u fa-tufti'" means that the affair of war is completed, as when a woman has nursed and then weaned, she has finished.]

He means war, and he used 'Ad as a metaphor for Thamud.

Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, We sent upon them a single cry﴾, meaning the cry of Jibril, peace be upon him. This has already passed in (Hud) [[See vol. 9, p. 61.]].

﴿So they became like the crushed refuse of the one who builds an enclosure﴾. Al-Hasan, Qatadah and Abu al-Aliyah read al-muhtaẓar with a fatha on the ẓa', meaning the enclosure itself. The rest read it with a kasra, meaning the owner of the enclosure. In as-Sihah it says: "al-muhtazir is the one who makes the enclosure." It is also read with the fatha, making it the object. It is said of a man of little good: "He is indeed a wretched enclosure-maker." Abu 'Ubayd said: I think he named his wealth an enclosure because he kept it held back and withheld it, and it is a form (fa'ila) meaning the passive participle (maf'ula). Al-Mahdawi said: Whoever reads the ẓa' of al-muhtazir with a fatha, it is a verbal noun, and the meaning is "like the crushed refuse of enclosing." It is also possible that al-muhtazir refers to the wood from which the enclosure is made. Ibn 'Abbas said: al-muhtazir is the man who makes an enclosure for his sheep out of trees and thorns; whatever falls from that and is trampled by the sheep is hashim. He said:

"They raised a dust cloud like the smoke of a fire,
blazing in old, crushed boxthorn."

And from him: "like grass eaten by sheep." And also from him: "like rotten bones that have been burned," which is the view of Qatadah. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it is the dust scattered from walls on a windy day. Sufyan al-Thawri said: it is what is scattered from the enclosure when you strike it with a stick; it is a form (fa'il) in the sense of a passive participle (maf'ul). Ibn Zayd said: The Arabs call everything that was moist and then dried out hashim. Al-hazr means prevention, and al-muhtazir is the one who does it (the iftial form). From it one says: "ihtazara 'ala ibilihi" and "hazara," meaning he gathered trees and placed some of them on top of others to protect his camels from the cold wind and from predators. The poet said:

"You see the carcasses of mounts on both sides of it,
as if their bones were dry wood of the crushed kind."

There is a proverb: "The last of them is the least in drink," and its origin is in watering camels, because the last of them comes to the water when the trough has already been drained. The meaning of "attended" (muhtadar) is that each one present is entitled to his share: the she-camel comes to the water on her day, and is absent from them on their day. This is what Muqatil said. Mujahid said: The people of Thamud would come to the water on the day of her absence and drink, and they would come to the milk on the day of her coming and milk her.

Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So they called their companion﴾, meaning: by urging him to hamstring her, ﴿and he took it in hand and hamstrung her﴾. The meaning of ta'aṭa is "to take up the action," from the expression 'aṭawtu, meaning "I reached out," and from it is the verse of Hassan:

"Both of them are the milkers of the juice, so hand me
a cup, the more relaxing of the two for the joints."

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: He lay in wait for her at the foot of a tree on her path and shot her with an arrow, which struck the muscle of her leg. Then he rushed at her with a sword and cut her hamstring, and she fell and cried out in a single cry, and her young one slid from her belly. Then he slaughtered her, and her young one ran off until it reached a rock at the top of a mountain, where it cried out and then took refuge in it. Then Salih, peace be upon him, came to them, and when he saw that the she-camel had been hamstrung, he wept and said: "You have violated the sanctity of Allah, so rejoice in the punishment of Allah." The explanation of this meaning has already passed in (al-A'raf) [[See vol. 7, p. 241.]]. "Before him, or after him, like Qudar, when peoples followed him
into error, and they perished."

The Arabs call the butcher "Qaddar," in likeness to Miqdar ibn Salif, the ill-omened one of the family of Thamud. Muhalhil said:

"We strike their heads with swords,
striking like the butcher striking the feast-offering of the travelers."
[Qaddar: the butcher. Naqi'a: what is slaughtered for hospitality. Qidam: those returning from a journey, plural of qadim. It is also said that qidam means a king. Another reading is: "We strike their heads with sharp swords."]

like the Red One of 'Ad; then she will suckle and wean."
[Tuntij lakum means war. "Ghilman ashʼam" means "boys of ill omen," or "all of them in ill omen like the Red One of 'Ad." "Thumma turdi'u fa-tufti'" means that the affair of war is completed, as when a woman has nursed and then weaned, she has finished.]

He said, may He be exalted: ﴿The people of Lot denied the warnings﴾. He informs about the people of Lot as well, when they denied Lot.

﴿Indeed, We sent upon them a violent wind (ḥāṣiban)﴾, that is, a wind that pelts them with pebbles (al-ḥaṣbāʾ), which are small stones. Al-Naḍr said: al-ḥāṣib is the ḥaṣbāʾ carried in the wind. *They were dragged over by their hems, after their people had gone away,*
*by every gusting wind that pelts with gravel.*

ʿAṣafat al-rīḥ means the wind grew violent, so it is a stormy wind (rīḥ ʿāṣif) and ʿaṣūf. Al-Farazdaq said:

*Facing the north of Syria, it strikes us*
*with a pelting wind, like scattered cotton fluff.*

﴿Except the family of Lot﴾, meaning those who followed him in his religion, and there were none except his two daughters. ﴿We saved them at dawn (bi-saḥar)﴾. Al-Akhfash said: it is declined (unṣarif) because it is indefinite. If he meant the dawn of a specific day, he would not decline it. ﴿Thus do We reward whoever gives thanks﴾, that is, whoever believes in God and obeys Him.

﴿And he had warned them﴾, meaning Lot warned them, ﴿of Our seizure (baṭshatanā)﴾, Our punishment and Our taking them with the chastisement. ﴿But they disputed the warnings﴾, that is, they doubted what the Messenger warned them of and did not believe him. It is a form of tafāʿul from al-miryah (doubt).

﴿And they sought to seduce him from his guests﴾, that is, they wanted him to hand over to them those angels who had come to him in the form of guests, seeking indecency, as mentioned earlier [[See vol. 9, p. 73.]]. It is said: "rāwadtuhu ʿalā kadhā murāwadatan wa rawādan," meaning I sought it from him. "Rāda al-kalaʾ yarūduhu rawdan wa riyādan," and "irtādahu irtiyādan" have the same meaning, that is, he sought it. In the hadith: "When one of you urinates, let him seek (fal-yartad) a place for his urine," meaning let him look for a soft or sloping place.

﴿So We blinded their eyes (faṭamasnā aʿyunahum)﴾. It is narrated that Jibril, peace be upon him, struck them with his wing and they became blind. It was also said: their eyes became like the rest of the face, with no visible opening, just as the wind obliterates signposts by blowing dust over them. ﴿So taste My punishment and My warnings﴾. That is, We said to them: taste. The meaning of this command is information, that is, We made them taste My punishment with which Lot had warned them.

﴿And in the morning there struck them a settled punishment (ʿadhābun mustaqirr)﴾, that is, a lasting, general punishment that settled upon them until it led them to the punishment of the Hereafter. That punishment was the overturning of their town upon them and making its top its bottom. Here "bukrah" is indefinite, which is why it is declined.

﴿So taste My punishment and My warnings﴾. The punishment that came down upon them, namely the obliteration of their eyes, is other than the punishment by which they were destroyed; therefore the repetition is fitting.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 54, verses 41–42:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And there had certainly come to the people of Pharaoh the warnings﴾. It means the Copts. "Al-nudhur" (the warnings) refers to Musa and Harun. The word in the plural form may be used for two.

(They denied Our signs) Our miracles that indicate Our oneness and the prophethood of Our prophets, and they are: the staff, the hand, the years of drought, the effacement, the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, and the blood. It is also said that "al-nudhur" (the warnings) means the messengers, for there came to them Yusuf and his sons, until Musa came to them. And it is said that "al-nudhur" means the warning itself.

(So We seized them with the seizing of One Almighty) i.e., Mighty in His retribution, (Omnipotent) i.e., Able to do whatever He wills.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 54, verse 43–46:
